region.text: Nagorno-Karabakh and the seven districts the Armenian side later held; the page names Khojaly

ledger.note: February 1992: the war for Nagorno-Karabakh becomes a ground campaign. 'In February 1992, Khojaly was captured by a mixed force of ethnic Armenians'. The page frames the war as 'the majority ethnic Armenians of Nagorno-Karabakh backed by Armenia, and the Republic of Azerbaijan', spanning 'February 1988 to May 1994', and dates no earlier ground campaign (Operation Ring in the Shahumyan region is undated). The zone is my reading: Nagorno-Karabakh plus the districts held after the ceasefire.

region.text: Lachin district, the corridor between Armenia and Nagorno-Karabakh

ledger.note: May 1992: Armenian forces take Lachin and open a corridor to Armenia; Azerbaijan loses control of the district. 'the next day Armenian forces took control of the town and opened a humanitarian corridor' (the Lachin offensive began on 18 May); a week earlier Shusha had fallen ('they managed to capture the town and force the Azerbaijanis to retreat on 9 May'). The page names the town; the district is my reading. Azerbaijan is the owner; the land stays in its de jure shape and is drawn hatched in the occupier's colour.

April 1993: Armenian forces take Kalbajar from Azerbaijan. 'By 3 April, Armenian forces were in possession of Kalbajar.' UN Security Council Resolution 822, passed 30 April, demanded 'the withdrawal of all occupying forces from Kalbajar'. The year is the section's (the quoted sentence carries no year); the Nagorno-Karabakh conflict page confirms 'Turkey closed its border with Armenia in April 1993 after Armenian forces captured Kalbajar.' Azerbaijan is the owner.

July 1993: Armenian forces take Agdam. The Aghdam page: 'Armenian forces captured Aghdam in July 1993'; the First Nagorno-Karabakh War page dates the bombardment ('On 4 July Armenian forces commenced an artillery bombardment on Agdam'). The page names the town; the region is the district (reviewer eu-19-g, 2026-10-31: date confirmed on the Aghdam page, confidence raised from 1). Azerbaijan is the owner.

region.text: Fuzuli and Jabrayil, 'two regions in Azerbaijan proper'

ledger.note: 23 August 1993: Armenian forces take Jabrayil and Fuzuli. The Jabrayil District page: 'The territory was occupied by Armenian forces on August 23, 1993'; the Fuzuli District page: 'the city of Fuzuli's occupation by Armenian forces on 23 August 1993'. The First Nagorno-Karabakh War page: 'In mid-August, Armenians massed a force to take Fuzuli and Jebrail'; in January 1994 Azerbaijan retook part of Fuzuli district but not the town. (Reviewer eu-19-g, 2026-10-31: date confirmed on the two district pages, confidence raised from 1.) Azerbaijan is the owner.

August 1993: Qubadli district falls. The Qubadli District page: 'The district came was seized by the breakaway Republic of Artsakh in August 1993 during the First Nagorno-Karabakh War.' The page names Artsakh, not Armenia, as the captor; the occupier is kept as in the other districts (see notes). (Reviewer eu-19-g, 2026-10-31: split from a 1994-05 confidence-1 event.) Azerbaijan is the owner.

29 October 1993: Zangilan district falls. The Zangilan District page: 'On October 29, 1993, the district came under the occupation of the Nagorno-Karabakh Defence Army'. The page names the Karabakh army, not Armenia's; the occupier is kept as in the other districts (see notes). (Reviewer eu-19-g, 2026-10-31: split from a 1994-05 confidence-1 event.) Azerbaijan is the owner.

region.text: Nagorno-Karabakh and the seven surrounding districts

ledger.note: 12 May 1994: the ceasefire ends the First Nagorno-Karabakh War. 'On 5 May, with Russia acting as a mediator, all parties agreed to cease hostilities', to take effect 'at 12:01 AM on 12 May'. By then 'the Armenians were in full control of the enclave, in addition to surrounding Azerbaijani territories'; the Armenia page: 'The first Karabakh war ended after a Russian-brokered ceasefire was concluded in 1994.'

1994: Nagorno-Karabakh becomes a de facto state outside Azerbaijan's control. The Azerbaijan page says it 'became de facto independent with the end of the First Nagorno-Karabakh War in 1994'; the Republic of Artsakh page gives the republic's proclamation as 2 September 1991 and its declaration of independence as 6 January 1992. Azerbaijan keeps it as de jure territory (the First Nagorno-Karabakh War page: UN Security Council Resolutions 874 and 884 'acknowledged Nagorno-Karabakh as a region of Azerbaijan'), so it is drawn hatched in the Artsakh colour. This is the southern part, the one Azerbaijan retook in 2020. The republic needs its own dossier (eu-19-x).

region.text: the rest of Nagorno-Karabakh around Stepanakert

ledger.note: 1994: Nagorno-Karabakh becomes a de facto state outside Azerbaijan's control ('became de facto independent with the end of the First Nagorno-Karabakh War in 1994', Azerbaijan page). Azerbaijan keeps it as de jure territory, drawn hatched in the Artsakh colour. This is the part that lasted until September 2023; the Republic of Artsakh page gives its infobox area as 11,458 km2 in 1995 and 3,170 km2 in 2021.

region.text: the southern districts and Shusha, taken in the 2020 fighting

ledger.note: 27 September 2020: Azerbaijan opens an offensive. 'Fighting began on the morning of 27 September, with an Azerbaijani offensive.' The zone is my reading from the places the page names (Jabrayil, Füzuli, Agbend, Shusha) and the Artsakh page's 'primarily in the southern part of the region'.

October 2020: Azerbaijan retakes Jabrayil and Fuzuli. 'Azerbaijan announced the capture of Jabrayil on 9 October 2020 and Füzuli on 17 October 2020.' These are announcements; the page does not add independent confirmation.

20 October 2020: Azerbaijan retakes Zangilan. The Zangilan District page: 'On 20 October 2020, the President of Azerbaijan, Ilham Aliyev, announced that Azerbaijani military forces recaptured' the district and Zangilan city; the Second Nagorno-Karabakh War page adds the capture of Agbend on 22 October 2020. An announcement, not independently confirmed. (Reviewer eu-19-g, 2026-10-31: split from the joint Qubadli-Zangilan event.)

October 2020: Azerbaijan retakes Qubadli. A national hero was 'killed during the operations in Qubadli District' (confirmed 23 October 2020); the page gives no capture date for the district; the Azerbaijan page says 'the seven districts and parts of Nagorno-Karabakh were returned to Azerbaijani control'. (Reviewer eu-19-g, 2026-10-31: Zangilan split off as its own event.)

region.text: Shusha, Hadrut and the southern part of Nagorno-Karabakh, retaken by Azerbaijan

ledger.note: 8 November 2020: Shusha falls and southern Nagorno-Karabakh is lost. 'On 8 November 2020, Azerbaijani forces seized Shusha.' The Republic of Artsakh page: Azerbaijan 'recaptured territories, primarily in the southern part of the region, as well as the strategic town of Shushi', with Hadrut 'now under Azerbaijani control'; the Second Nagorno-Karabakh War infobox: 'Azerbaijan gains control of 72% of the Republic of Artsakh's territory'. The extent of the southern part is my reading from Natural Earth rayons.

10 November 2020: the ceasefire ends the Second Nagorno-Karabakh War. 'It was signed on 9 November by the President of Azerbaijan Ilham Aliyev, the Prime Minister of Armenia Nikol Pashinyan and the President of Russia Vladimir Putin', ending hostilities 'from 00:00, on 10 November 2020 Moscow time'. About 2,000 Russian peacekeepers deploy along the line of contact and the Lachin corridor.
20 November 2020: Armenia hands Agdam back. 'The Agdam District shall be returned to the Republic of Azerbaijan by 20 November 2020.' The page does not report whether the date was met.

25 November 2020: Armenia hands Kalbajar back. 'The Republic of Armenia shall return the Kalbajar District to the Republic of Azerbaijan by 15 November 2020'; 'On 15 November, at Armenia's request, Azerbaijan extended the deadline' by 10 days, 'until 25 November'. The page does not report the handover itself.

1 December 2020: Armenia hands Lachin back. '...and the Lachin District by 1 December 2020.' The 5 km Lachin corridor stays 'under the control of the Russian Federation peacemaking forces' (a strip, not drawn). The page does not report the handover itself.

region.text: the Nagorno-Karabakh rump held by Artsakh

ledger.note: 19-20 September 2023: Artsakh surrenders and Azerbaijan takes the rest of Nagorno-Karabakh. 'On 19 September, Azerbaijan launched a military offensive into Artsakh-controlled territory. The following day, the government of the Republic of Artsakh agreed to disarm and a ceasefire took effect.' On 28 September 2023 its president signed a decree to dissolve all institutions by 1 January 2024; the Azerbaijan page dates the 'reintegration of Artsakh' to 1 January 2024. The Armenia page adds that the ceasefire was reached 'at the mediation of the Russian peacekeeping command'.

wars.outcome: Armenian-backed forces took Nagorno-Karabakh and, in 1992-1994, the districts around it (about 9% of Azerbaijan outside the enclave); a Russian-brokered ceasefire took effect at 12:01 AM on 12 May 1994 and the Republic of Artsakh stayed 'de facto independent but internationally unrecognized'.
wars.note: The war began in February 1988, before either republic existed as a state; the dossiers cover it from 1991 and the ledger's contest zone from February 1992 (Khojaly). The 1994 ceasefire left the land in Armenian-backed hands; the ledger draws the districts as occupation and Nagorno-Karabakh proper as the Republic of Artsakh.

wars.name: Second Nagorno-Karabakh War

zones.text: the southern districts (Jabrayil, Fuzuli, Zangilan, Qubadli) and Shusha and Hadrut, where the 2020 fighting took ground

wars.outcome: Azerbaijan retook Jabrayil, Füzuli and Shusha (named on the page) and, by the Azerbaijan and Artsakh pages' wording, the rest of the southern districts and Hadrut ('72% of the disputed territory'); the ceasefire of 9/10 November 2020 obliged Armenia to hand Agdam, Kalbajar and Lachin back by 20 November, 25 November and 1 December and put about 2,000 Russian peacekeepers on the line of contact and the Lachin corridor.
wars.note: Ceasefire page (second source): Agdam by 20 November, Kalbajar extended from 15 to 25 November, Lachin by 1 December 2020.

wars.name: September 2022 Armenia–Azerbaijan clashes
wars.outcome: 'Azerbaijani troops taking control of strategic positions deep inside Armenia'; the infobox puts the Armenian territory Azerbaijan occupies at 200 km2, after about 41 km2 taken on 12 May 2021 in Syunik and Gegharkunik. A ceasefire was brokered on 14 September 2022.
wars.note: Not drawn: 41 to 200 km2 is under one cell of the grid (about 253 km2) and the pages name provinces, not the strips. A gap-filler could add a border strip once the gazetteer can name it. The opened page is thin on where the positions lie.

wars.name: 2023 Azerbaijani offensive in Nagorno-Karabakh

zones.text: the rest of Nagorno-Karabakh around Stepanakert (Natural Earth rayons Stepanakert/Xankəndi, Xocalı and Tərtər, approximate; held until September 2023)

wars.outcome: 19-20 September 2023: Azerbaijan's offensive ended in Artsakh's agreement to disarm; its president signed a decree on 28 September 2023 to dissolve all institutions by 1 January 2024.
wars.note: The Artsakh page has no separate article here; the Azerbaijan page dates the 'dissolution and reintegration of Artsakh' to 1 January 2024. Armenia is not named as a belligerent in the sentences read.

certainty.note: The war years: the front in and around Nagorno-Karabakh moved month by month; Azerbaijan's other frontiers (Turkey, Iran, Georgia, Russia) were Soviet-era lines, sharp.

Soviet republic boundaries and the 1994 ceasefire line of contact, then the 2020 ceasefire lines. The Armenia-Azerbaijan frontier itself stays undelimited on the pages read, and the strips Azerbaijan holds in Armenia since 2021 are not mapped, so that frontier is the exception.

notes:
Page budget: the brief allows 1-2 pages for a 3-shape state; eight pages were opened because the border moves here (1992-94, 2020, 2023) are only dated on the Karabakh war pages, shared with the Armenia dossier, where the same ledger appears with owner and occupier swapped. Opened: Azerbaijan, First Nagorno-Karabakh War, Nagorno-Karabakh conflict, Second Nagorno-Karabakh War, 2020 Nagorno-Karabakh ceasefire agreement, Republic of Artsakh, September 2022 Armenia-Azerbaijan clashes, Armenia.

SAME STATE OR NOT: Cliopatria's 'Azerbaijan Democratic Republic' (1918-1919, slug azerbaijan-democratic-republic, another eu-19 part) and 'Republic of Azerbaijan' (1992-2024) share Wikidata Q227 but are different states with the Soviet period between (the Azerbaijan SSR has its own dossier, 1920-1991). This dossier is only the republic since October 1991, with the SSR as predecessor.

MODEL (for the colour and rendering agents): Azerbaijan's shape is its whole de jure territory, Nakhchivan and Nagorno-Karabakh included, in every year (86,600 km2). Cliopatria cuts the Armenian-held land out for 1992-2024 (78,526 km2 in 1992-95, 70,479 km2 in 1996-2023 and again in 2024), which is stale from 2020 and wrong in 2024; the pages call the seven districts 'Armenian-occupied territories' (Second Nagorno-Karabakh War infobox) and the UN resolutions it quotes speak of 'occupying forces', so the land is kept in the shape and drawn through events: contest_start 1992-02 / contest_end 1994-05 and 2020-09 / 2020-11; occupation_start / occupation_end for the seven districts (Armenia the occupier, Azerbaijan the owner here; Lachin 1992-05 and Kalbajar 1993-04 are dated, Agdam, Fuzuli, Jabrayil, Qubadli and Zangilan are confidence 1 because the pages do not date their fall; they end with the October 2020 captures and the November-December 2020 handovers); and for Nagorno-Karabakh itself an occupation pair with counterpart republic-of-artsakh from 1994-05 (the Azerbaijan page: 'became de facto independent with the end of the First Nagorno-Karabakh War in 1994'), southern part ended 2020-11, rump ended 2023-09. The Artsakh pair assumes the slug republic-of-artsakh (see below).

NEEDS A DOSSIER (eu-19-x): republic-of-artsakh, the de facto Republic of Artsakh, proclaimed 2 September 1991, independence declared 6 January 1992, capital Stepanakert, 11,458 km2 in 1995 and 3,170 km2 in 2021, institutions dissolved by decree of 28 September 2023 with effect 1 January 2024.

NOT DRAWN: Azerbaijan's positions inside Armenia since 12 May 2021 (about 41 km2) and after 12-14 September 2022 ('over 200 square kilometers' of Armenian land): the pages name Syunik and Gegharkunik, not strips, and 200 km2 is under one grid cell (253 km2). The 2021-2022 border crisis article did not load under four titles (see the report's pages_failed). Not covered by any opened page: the Azerbaijani enclaves in Armenia and Artsvashen, the 2024 Tavush border transfers, the Russian and Georgian boundary treaties; the Azerbaijan page gives only border lengths (390 km Russia, 756 km Iran, 480 km Georgia). A gap-filler should open the district pages (Agdam, Fuzuli, Jabrayil, Qubadli, Zangilan) for the 1993 capture dates, and the Lachin corridor/blockade (12 December 2022) is on the Artsakh page only.

AREA CHECK: infobox 86,600 km2 (no year). Cliopatria 78,526 / 70,479 / 70,479 km2, ratios 0.91 / 0.81 / 0.81. The excess outside the country in the 1992 shape (eight cells) is gazetteer noise.

GAZETTEER: Natural Earth lacks the Lachin district ('Laçın'), Hadrut, Askeran and Martakert (Ağdərə); Nagorno-Karabakh is approximated by the rayons Stepanakert, Xocalı, Xocavənd, Şuşa and Tərtər. The admin1 'Naxçıvan' is one cell (the city), the autonomous republic is the region 'Nakhchivan' (21 cells).

DATE DISAGREEMENT: the Azerbaijan page has the 30 August 1991 proclamation, the 18 October 1991 Declaration of Independence and recognition on 26 December 1991; start is 1991-10, matching the SSR dossier's end.

REVIEW eu-19-g (2026-10-31): the five district capture dates were confirmed on the district pages and the events re-dated: Agdam July 1993, Fuzuli and Jabrayil 23 August 1993, Qubadli August 1993, Zangilan 29 October 1993 (the joint 1994-05 Qubadli-Zangilan event was split, and its 2020 end with it: Zangilan 20 October 2020); confidence raised from 1 to 2. The Qubadli and Zangilan pages name Artsakh's army as the captor.
